Definition: Percentage of individuals who used the internet (from any location, via any device) in the last three months. This measures actual internet adoption beyond network availability, capturing the combined effect of infrastructure, affordability, digital literacy, and relevance.
Comments: World Bank (WDI IT.NET.USER.ZS) shows individuals using the Internet at 27.6% of population in 2022, also reflected in DataReportal (internet penetration 27.6% Jan 2024 referencing latest published data).
revision_notes: Confirmed. ITU DataHub reports Somalia's internet usage rate at 27.9% of the population for 2024. World Bank/ITU WDI series shows 27.6% for 2022, consistent with the cited DataReportal (27.6%, Jan 2024) and Trading Economics figures. All estimates sit within the 15-29% band, supporting the existing Value Code 2.
revised_comments: ITU data puts Somalia's internet usage rate at approximately 27.9% of the population in 2024, consistent with World Bank/ITU estimates of 27.6% for 2022 and DataReportal's Digital 2024 report. This places usage in the 15-29% range.

Definition: Affordability of electricity for residential and small business consumers, measured as cost of electricity relative to income levels. High electricity costs are a direct barrier to ICT adoption and data center viability.
Value Name: Very Expensive (>10% of household income for basic service)
Comments: Tariffs reported to range 50–125 US cents/kWh in Somalia (very high) per ITA; this implies very expensive electricity relative to income; used as affordability proxy.
revision_notes: Confirmed. US Trade.gov Country Commercial Guide (updated Jan 2024) reports tariffs of 50-125 US cents/kWh, among the highest in Africa. Ecofin Agency (Jan 2026), citing World Bank data, reports an average electricity cost of about US$0.61/kWh in 2023, with prices exceeding US$1/kWh in areas served by private diesel generators, versus US$0.15/kWh in Kenya and US$0.06/kWh in Ethiopia. Given Somalia's very low GNI per capita (around US$500), these tariffs represent a very high share of household income for basic electricity service, supporting Value Code 1 (Very Expensive).
revised_comments: Electricity in Somalia is among the most expensive in Africa, averaging around US$0.61 per kWh in 2023 and exceeding US$1 per kWh in areas served by private diesel micro-grids, compared with roughly US$0.15 in Kenya and US$0.06 in Ethiopia. Given Somalia's very low household incomes, this represents a very high share of income for basic electricity service.

Definition: Whether the country has established policies, regulations, and programmes supporting off-grid and distributed energy solutions (mini-grids, solar home systems). These are critical for extending ICT infrastructure to unserved areas beyond the central grid.
Comments: Somalia has active off-grid/standalone solar programming support (Somali Electricity Access Project provides grants and incentives for solar home systems; Rural Electrification Strategy focused on stand-alone solar is being developed with MoEWR/ACE TAF support).
revision_notes: Confirmed and refreshed. IRENA's 2025 Energy Transition Assessment for Somalia finds the country is updating electricity sector legislation and institutions but has 'yet to operationalise these structures or establish the necessary enforcement and compliance mechanisms.' UNDP/GEF's Africa Mini-grids Programme is developing a National Mini-grid Policy and Regulation (validation workshop Oct 2025), and active off-grid deployment continues, including an AfDB-funded solar/grid programme in Bosaso, a planned 55 MWp hybrid solar plant for Mogadishu, and a Jan 2026 tender for off-grid solar at 22 health centres. This is consistent with 'Active policy with some deployment' (Value Code 3); 'Comprehensive framework' (4) is not yet supported as the policy/regulatory framework remains unoperationalised.
revised_comments: Somalia has an active but still-developing off-grid energy policy landscape. The Ministry of Energy and Water Resources, with UNDP/GEF support through the Africa Mini-grids Programme, is developing a National Mini-grid Policy and Regulation, while deployment continues through projects such as an AfDB-backed solar and grid programme in Bosaso, a planned hybrid solar plant for Mogadishu, and tenders for off-grid solar at health facilities. The legal and regulatory framework is still being operationalised rather than fully enforced.

Definition: Percentage of total electricity generation from renewable sources (hydro, solar, wind, geothermal, biomass). Indicates energy sustainability and potential for distributed power solutions relevant to ICT infrastructure in off-grid areas.
revision_notes: The cited Ecofin figure ('<10%, diesel 80%+') describes diesel's share of installed generation capacity (350-400 MW in 2023, per IRENA/World Bank), not actual generation output, so it does not directly support a generation-share code. Actual generation data from the Africa Energy Portal show Somalia generating 93 GWh from renewables against 396 GWh from fossil fuels in 2023 (about 19% renewable), and EIA-derived data (via statbase.org) show renewable generation rising from 72.2 GWh in 2023 to 81.5 GWh in 2024. Both independently indicate a renewable generation share above the 10% threshold, in the 10-24% band. Recalculated from Value Code 1 to Value Code 2. Flagged for human review because the underlying figures come from secondary aggregators (Africa Energy Portal, EIA-derived statbase) rather than a single authoritative primary generation-mix statistic, and the two sources diverge somewhat (15% vs 19%).
revised_comments: Renewable sources, chiefly solar, are estimated to account for around 15-20% of Somalia's electricity generation, with diesel generation still dominant. Africa Energy Portal data show renewable generation of around 93 GWh against 396 GWh from fossil fuels in 2023, while EIA-derived estimates show renewable output rising from about 72 GWh in 2023 to 82 GWh in 2024. Somalia's solar sector continues to expand through health-facility electrification, hybrid mini-grids, and larger urban solar-plus-storage projects such as the planned Mogadishu hybrid plant.
